explication:
<explanation>
1. Identify the project type and purpose  
   - This is an open-source, command-line Python library for running standard benchmarks (“evals”) against large language models and reporting accuracy.  
   - Purpose: Provide a lightweight, extensible framework to run zero-shot and chain-of-thought evaluations (MMLU, MATH, GPQA, etc.) via different model APIs (OpenAI, Claude).

2. Analyze the file structure  
   - Top-level Python modules (e.g., mmlu_eval.py, math_eval.py, …): one module per benchmark.  
   - simple_evals.py (entry point): discovers evals, parses CLI args, orchestrates runs.  
   - common.py, types.py: shared types, data-structures, helper functions.  
   - sampler/ (package): abstraction layer for model sampling, with concrete classes for OpenAI chat completion, Claude, etc.  
   - healthbench_scripts/: Jupyter notebook for analysis of HealthBench results (ancillary).  
   - Configuration: .gitignore, LICENSE, README.md.

3. Examine the README for additional insights  
   - CLI usage: `python -m simple-evals.simple_evals --model <name> --examples <n>`  
   - Supports injecting different samplers via environment variables (e.g., OPENAI_API_KEY, ANTHROPIC_API_KEY).  
   - Evals discover benchmark definitions, load prompt templates, call sampler to get model outputs, compute metrics (accuracy, F1).

4. How to create the system design diagram  
   a. Main components  
     • CLI Interface (simple_evals.py)  
     • Evaluation Manager / Orchestrator (shared logic in simple_evals + common.py)  
     • Benchmark Modules (mmlu_eval, math_eval, …)  
     • Sampler Interface (sampler/chat_completion_sampler.py, claude_sampler.py, etc.)  
     • External Model APIs (OpenAI API, Anthropic Claude API)  
     • Result Aggregator & Reporter (prints tables, writes markdown)  
     • (Optional) Analysis Notebook (healthbench_scripts)  
   b. Relationships & data flow  
     1. User invokes CLI.  
     2. CLI parses arguments, selects benchmark modules.  
     3. For each example in each eval:  
        – Orchestrator calls Benchmark Module to load prompt & ground truth.  
        – Benchmark Module calls Sampler Interface (via common abstractions).  
        – Sampler sends API requests to external LLM service.  
        – LLM returns completion; Sampler returns it to Benchmark Module.  
        – Benchmark Module computes metric (e.g., accuracy, F1).  
        – Result is sent back to Orchestrator.  
     4. Orchestrator aggregates results across examples & benchmarks.  
     5. CLI outputs formatted tables (console, markdown).  
   c. Architectural patterns / principles  
     - Plugin-style discovery: each eval and sampler is a module conforming to a shared interface.  
     - Clear separation of concerns: eval logic vs. sampling vs. reporting.  
     - Dependency injection via environment variables and dynamic imports.  
   d. Key technologies / libraries  
     - Python 3, standard library (argparse, importlib)  
     - HTTP clients (requests or underlying OpenAI/Anthropic SDKs)  
     - Jupyter for analysis (optional)  
     - Markdown rendering for result tables  

5. Tailoring the diagram for this open-source evaluation tool  
   - Emphasize the core plugin architecture: show “Eval Modules” and “Sampler Modules” as interchangeable components.  
   - Highlight extensibility points: where to add a new eval or a new sampler.  
   - Show integration with external services (OpenAI, Claude) as “black-box” services.  

6. Diagramming guidelines  
   - Use distinct shapes/colors:  
     • Rectangles for internal components (CLI, Orchestrator, Eval Modules, Samplers)  
     • Cylinders for data stores or datasets (benchmark datasets, ground truth)  
     • Cloud icons for external APIs (OpenAI, Claude)  
   - Label every component clearly.  
   - Draw directional arrows for data/control flow:  
     – CLI → Orchestrator → Eval Module → Sampler → External API  
     – External API → Sampler → Eval Module → Orchestrator → CLI  
   - Color-code: e.g., blue for core framework, green for plugins, orange for external services.  

7. Level of detail  
   - Show each eval module as a separate box or group them under “Benchmark Plugins.”  
   - Show sampler package broken into interfaces and concrete adapters.  
   - Include the optional analysis notebook as a side component for post-run visualization.  

By following this structure, the diagram will capture all essential architectural elements—entry point, plugin modules, API adapters, data flow, and reporting—while making it clear where new benchmarks or samplers can be plugged in.  
</explanation>
